indicator.subject: Science
indicator.content_standard: B2.4.1.1: Demonstrate understanding of the concept of energy, its various forms, sources and the ways in which it can be transformed and conserved

skills.description: Name the source of energy for everyday activities
Explain what happens when energy is missing

misconceptions: Only people need energy; machines and animals do not.
Food is not energy; it is just something we eat.
Energy is something you can always see.
A car at rest has no energy at all.

questions.stem: Which of these everyday activities requires energy?
hints: You move your body a lot.
You get tired after doing it.
questions.explanation: Running requires a lot of energy because your body is working hard to move.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think sitting or sleeping require no energy at all.

questions.stem: Where do people get the energy to walk and work?
questions.explanation: People get energy from the food they eat.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think people get energy directly from the sun like plants.

questions.stem: Which of these household items uses energy to work?
hints: It needs to be plugged in.
questions.explanation: A television uses electrical energy to work.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think all household items require energy.

questions.stem: What gives a car the energy to move?
hints: You buy it at a filling station.
questions.explanation: A car gets its energy from petrol (fuel).
questions.misconception: Pupils may think cars run on water.

questions.stem: What happens to a person who has not eaten all day?
questions.explanation: A person who has not eaten has no energy from food and will feel weak.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think skipping food gives you energy.

questions.stem: Ama is pounding fufu. What is she using to do this work?
questions.explanation: Ama is using energy from her body (which comes from the food she eats) to pound the fufu.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not connect physical work to body energy.

questions.stem: What is the main source of energy for plants to make their own food?
hints: It is in the sky during the day.
questions.explanation: Plants use energy from the sun (sunlight) to make their food.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think plants only get energy from the soil.

questions.stem: What happens to a torch when its battery runs out?
questions.explanation: A torch needs energy from the battery to give light. When the battery runs out, it stops working.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think a torch can work without a battery.

questions.stem: Which of these activities does NOT use much energy?
questions.explanation: Sleeping uses much less energy than active tasks like running or playing.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think sleeping uses the same energy as playing.

questions.stem: Kwame plugs in an electric iron. What source of energy is he using?
hints: It comes from the wall socket.
questions.explanation: Kwame is using electrical energy from the socket to heat the iron.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think an iron uses fire.

questions.stem: Name one activity you did today that used energy.
questions.explanation: Walking, writing, and playing all require energy from your body.
questions.misconception: Pupils may name a passive activity like sleeping.

questions.stem: What gives you energy to play football?
questions.explanation: Food gives you the energy you need to play football.
questions.misconception: Pupils may say they get energy from water only.

questions.stem: Why does a fan need electricity to work?
options: To give it the energy to spin
hints: The motor makes the blades spin.
questions.explanation: A fan needs electrical energy to power its motor and make the blades spin.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think fans create cold energy out of nowhere.

questions.stem: What would happen to a moving car if the driver suddenly turned off the engine (with no fuel going in)?
options: It would turn into a bicycle
hints: The engine provides the energy to move.
Without energy, it cannot keep moving.
questions.explanation: Without the engine providing energy from fuel, the car would eventually slow down and stop.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think a car can move forever without fuel.

questions.stem: A farmer uses a cutlass to clear grass. What provides the energy for the cutlass to move?
questions.explanation: The farmer's muscles (body energy) provide the force and energy to swing the cutlass.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think tools have their own energy.

questions.stem: Explain how a person gets the energy to run a race.

criteria.description: Mentions the body using energy from food to run

hints: What do athletes eat before a race?
Where does body energy come from?
questions.explanation: A person eats food, which gives their body energy. The body uses this energy to run.

questions.stem: Explain what happens in a community when the electricity supply goes off for a whole day.

criteria.description: States that electrical appliances will not work
States that activities requiring electricity will stop (e.g., fridges get warm, no lights)

hints: What things in your house need electricity?
What happens to food in the fridge?
questions.explanation: When electricity goes off, appliances like fridges, fans, and lights stop working, disrupting daily life.

questions.stem: Why is the sun considered the ultimate source of energy for almost all living things?
options: Because it gives light and heat, which plants use to make food that animals and humans eat
hints: Plants use sunlight to make food.
Where does the food chain start?
questions.explanation: The sun provides light and warmth that plants need to make food. Animals and humans eat these plants (or eat animals that ate the plants), so the sun is the ultimate source of energy.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not understand the food chain link to the sun.

questions.stem: Ama says 'My car at rest has no energy.' Why is she wrong?
options: Because the car has fuel stored in its tank which is potential energy
hints: What is in the fuel tank?
Can the car move if you start the engine?
questions.explanation: A car at rest still has stored energy (in the fuel). This stored energy can be turned into movement when the engine starts.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think only moving objects have energy.

questions.stem: Tell your teacher two ways you use energy at home and two ways you use energy at school.

criteria.description: Names a second valid home activity
Names a second valid school activity

hints: Think about sweeping, cooking, or washing.
Think about writing, running, or carrying a bag.
questions.explanation: This tests the ability to identify everyday applications of energy in different settings.
